activities.name: Responsive Voice Turns
activities.prepare: A calm, softly lit caregiving space and an unhurried presence.
steps: Speak in a natural, warm voice around feedings, diaper changes, and cuddles
Watch for your baby's tiny sounds or shifts in expression
Pause quietly to leave room for a reply
activities.observe: Facial expressions, brief gazes, body movements, vocal shifts, and early tired cues.
activities.pause: Yawning, turning away, fussing, or heavy eyelids—dial back stimulation and tend to comfort.
activities.safety: Skip loud voices, sudden looming, or trying to hold their gaze longer than they want.

activities.name: Familiar Faces & Expressions
activities.prepare: A wakeful, comfortable baby; bring your face close at a gentle distance.
steps: Share natural expressions and soft, unhurried words
Let your baby's gaze—looking toward you or glancing away—guide how long you linger
activities.observe: Willingness to meet your eyes briefly and small spontaneous shifts—no set duration needed.
activities.pause: Wrap up whenever they keep looking away or seem uncomfortable.
activities.safety: Avoid bright flashing lights or sudden loud sounds.

activities.name: Gentle Holding & Soothing
activities.prepare: A steady hold with gentle support for your baby's head and neck.
steps: Answer hunger, tiredness, or discomfort cues promptly
Offer a familiar hold, a soft voice, and a quieter room
activities.observe: How your baby settles and whether feeding and rest needs are met.
activities.pause: Reach out to a doctor for persistent unusual crying, changes in breathing or color, or feeding trouble.
activities.safety: Avoid falling asleep holding your baby on a sofa or chair; always move them to a safe sleep space.

activities.name: Gradual Awake Tummy Time
activities.prepare: A firm, clean floor mat or approved play surface, with an adult right beside them.
steps: Try brief stretches when your baby is awake and content
Adjust duration gently based on how your baby responds
Use your voice and face nearby to invite natural head lifting and turning
activities.observe: Comfort, posture shifts, and active efforts—single-session length is never a test.
activities.pause: Stop right away if they cry hard, tire, or show unusual breathing or posture, and check with your doctor if needed.
activities.safety: Always place baby on their back for sleep; follow pediatric guidance for any special medical needs.

activities.name: Short Reads & Voice Company
activities.prepare: A simple picture book, a single image, or a familiar rhyme while seated comfortably.
steps: Describe one picture, recite a short rhyme, or talk softly about your day
Stop whenever your baby shows signs of tiredness
activities.observe: How they relax into a familiar voice, brief gazes, and soothing cues.
activities.pause: Wrap up if they turn away, fuss, or are ready for sleep.
activities.safety: Keep books and soft items out of the baby's sleep space.

activities.name: Awake Cues & Care Notes
activities.prepare: A notebook or a shared family note.
steps: Jot down one moment your baby reached out, one tired cue, and how you responded
Once a week, check in briefly on safety, caregiver energy, and any questions for your doctor
activities.observe: Shifts in your baby's curiosity, daily rhythms, and how sustainable your care routine feels.
activities.pause: Keep notes lighter if logging feels heavy; seek medical advice directly for any health red flags.
activities.safety: Home notes never replace well-child visits or standardized developmental screening.

activities.name: Face-to-Face Sound Turns
activities.prepare: A quiet moment and your warm, attentive face.
steps: Meet face-to-face while your baby is alert and content
Speak a short phrase or gently echo their sounds
Pause
Answer their sounds, smiles, or glances
activities.observe: Eye contact, vocalizing, natural pauses, and joyful back-and-forth.
activities.pause: Looking away, fussing, or clear signs of tiredness.
activities.safety: Skip bright lights, loud noises, or nonstop tickling and teasing.

activities.name: Narrating Everyday Care
activities.prepare: Everyday care moments—diapering, handwashing, dressing.
steps: Name what you are about to do before you begin
Wait for a glance, sound, or tiny movement in reply
As your child grows, add simple choices and invite them to help
activities.observe: Steady attention, early coos, or words joining in.
activities.pause: Tiredness or pulling away from touch.
activities.safety: Care safety comes first—never leave your child unattended during baths or diaper changes.

activities.name: Awake Tummy Play
activities.prepare: A firm, flat floor mat and your close company.
steps: Place on a safe, flat floor only while awake
Stay right beside them on the floor
Connect with your voice and smile at eye level
Build up brief, comfortable sessions over time
activities.observe: Head and neck control, propping on forearms, and overall comfort.
activities.pause: Unusual breathing, persistent crying, or clear discomfort.
activities.safety: Always place baby on their back to sleep; never do tummy time on high surfaces or soft beds.

activities.name: Watching Hands & Reaching
activities.prepare: A lightweight, baby-safe toy with no small parts.
steps: Set the toy where your baby can easily see it
Wait for them to reach on their own
Brush it gently near their palm or set it close, inviting them to grasp
activities.observe: Watching their own hands, batting, grasping, and exploring.
activities.safety: Check toys regularly for loose or worn parts.

activities.name: Following Gentle Sounds
activities.prepare: Your own voice or a soft, gentle rattle.
steps: Call softly or make a gentle sound within view and watch for a natural head turn
Respond warmly without turning it into a test
activities.observe: Listening, gazing, and turning toward the sound.
activities.safety: Keep sounds soft and away from the ears; never use headphones.

activities.name: One-Page Picture Reading
activities.prepare: A sturdy board book or simple picture card.
steps: Open to a single page
Point to whatever catches your baby's eye
Describe it in a few warm words
Pause for a look, reach, or coo
Close the book whenever their interest moves on
activities.observe: Gazing, patting the page, and shared attention.
activities.safety: Choose books with smooth edges and no peel-off pieces.

activities.name: Rhymes & Gentle Fingerplay
activities.prepare: A familiar lullaby, folk rhyme, or fingerplay you love.
steps: Pick a short, rhythmic rhyme
Pair it with warm expressions or gentle finger movements
Pause to wait for a smile, sound, or movement
Return to the same favorite tunes over many days
activities.observe: Delight, anticipation, and playful imitation.
activities.safety: Keep all movements gentle—never shake a baby.

activities.name: Safe Texture Discovery
activities.prepare: Clean, baby-safe cloths and large toys with different textures.
steps: Offer just one or two textures at a time
Let your baby touch and explore at their own pace
Name how it feels—soft, smooth, bumpy
Watch whether they want to keep exploring
activities.observe: Touching, releasing, and safe mouthing.
activities.safety: Avoid shedding fabrics, tiny pieces, and thin plastic bags.

activities.name: Mirror Faces Together
activities.prepare: A securely mounted, shatterproof baby mirror.
steps: Look into the mirror together
Answer your baby's smiles and expressions
Point to the faces you see
Enjoy the moment without expecting self-recognition
activities.observe: Studying faces, smiling, and babbling.
activities.safety: Ensure the mirror is firmly secured, shatterproof, and free of small trims.

activities.name: Listening to the Outdoors
activities.prepare: A safe stroller or carrier, and a quiet spot with trees or birdsong.
steps: Step outside when the weather feels comfortable
Name the sights and sounds around you—breeze, leaves, birds
Head back in whenever your baby seems ready
activities.observe: Curiosity and calm absorption.
activities.pause: Harsh sun, chill or heat, or signs of tiredness.
activities.safety: Watch for sun protection, air quality, and nearby traffic.

activities.name: Passing Hand to Hand
activities.prepare: An easy-to-grasp, baby-safe toy.
steps: Offer one toy within easy reach
Let your baby hold, turn, and pass it between hands freely
Skip nudging them to switch hands
activities.observe: Steady grasping and spontaneous hand-to-hand transfers.
activities.safety: Make sure the toy has no detachable small parts.

activities.name: Peekaboo Hands
activities.prepare: Just your two hands.
steps: Cover your own face with your hands, pause a beat, then reappear
Repeat softly with a warm smile
Let your baby set the rhythm for more or all done
activities.observe: Anticipation, giggles, and tracking your face.
activities.safety: Never cover your baby's face or airway.

activities.name: Tapping & Making Sounds
activities.prepare: Soft, sturdy blocks or large baby-safe objects to tap.
steps: Tap two pieces together gently to show the sound
Pause and listen together
Hand them over for your baby to explore freely
Describe the sounds—soft, loud, fast, slow
activities.observe: Repeating on purpose and comparing sounds.
activities.safety: Skip glass, sharp metal edges, or loose pieces.

activities.name: In and Out of a Basket
activities.prepare: A shallow basket and large, choking-safe household items or blocks.
steps: Show placing one large object into the basket
Wait for your child to reach in and take it out
Name the actions simply—"in," "out"
activities.observe: Emptying, filling, and joyful repetition.
activities.safety: Never use marbles, buttons, batteries, or small objects.

activities.name: Free Floor Exploration
activities.prepare: A clear, baby-proofed floor area.
steps: Clear away hazards and clutter
Place a favorite safe object a short reach away
Give unhurried space to roll, pivot, scoot, or crawl their own way
activities.observe: Self-initiated position changes and determined movement.
activities.safety: Never force sitting, standing, or walking; stay close and watchful.

activities.name: Follow Their Gaze & Name
activities.prepare: Everyday objects around your home.
steps: Notice whatever catches your child's eye
Name it plainly in a warm voice
Pause for a sound, point, or word
Repeat naturally alongside what you are doing
activities.observe: Pointing, shared glances, babbling, and early words.
activities.safety: Skip rapid-fire quizzing or demanding they repeat words.

activities.name: Everyday Gestures & Signs
activities.prepare: Action songs and real everyday moments.
steps: Model waving, pointing, or clapping in real context
Respond warmly to any gesture they offer
Welcome however your child chooses to communicate
activities.observe: Spontaneous gestures and shared attention.
activities.safety: Never pull or manipulate your child's arms to make them do a gesture.

activities.name: Rolling a Soft Ball
activities.prepare: A soft, easy-to-hold ball.
steps: Sit on the floor a short distance apart and roll the ball over
Wait for your child to touch, catch, or push it back
Build up back-and-forth turns naturally
activities.observe: Tracking the ball and pushing it back.
activities.safety: Choose an age-appropriate ball too large to mouth-choke, away from stairs.

activities.name: Stacking Chunky Blocks
activities.prepare: Large, sturdy wooden or soft blocks.
steps: Stack one or two blocks slowly to show
Step back and let your child try
When it tumbles, describe what happened and invite another try
activities.observe: Self-directed building and trying again.
activities.safety: Avoid small choking-sized blocks or tall towers that could tip and hurt.

activities.name: Wiping & Tidying Together
activities.prepare: A clean, child-sized cloth and a low, sturdy basket.
steps: Show one small movement, like wiping a tabletop
Hand your child their own small cloth
Let them try in their own way without correcting
activities.observe: Eager imitation and joy in pitching in.
activities.safety: Keep cleaning sprays, hot water, and sharp tools well out of reach.

activities.name: Two Simple Choices
activities.prepare: Two safe, acceptable clothes or toys.
steps: Hold up two options you are happy with
Ask a short, clear question
Wait for a word, point, or reach
activities.observe: Confidently showing a preference.
activities.safety: Make sure both choices are genuinely safe and doable.

activities.name: Matching Pictures & Objects
activities.prepare: Familiar household objects and matching picture cards.
steps: Start with just one familiar object and its picture
Show placing the object beside the card
Invite your child to try if they seem curious
activities.observe: Curiosity, focus, and imitation.
activities.safety: Ensure cards have no small detachable pieces.

activities.name: Turning Pages & Pointing
activities.prepare: A board book or large picture book.
steps: Let your child choose the book
Follow their finger and talk about what they point to
Welcome skipped pages, favorite repeats, or stopping early
activities.observe: Pointing to pictures, turning pages, and chiming in.
activities.pause: Wandering away from the reading spot.
activities.safety: Skip forcing them to sit still or quizzing them on every page.

activities.name: Free Scribbling with Chunky Crayons
activities.prepare: Chunky, non-toxic crayons and a large sheet of paper.
steps: Tape or steady the paper on a flat surface
Make one or two relaxed strokes to show
Let your child make marks freely
Describe the colors and lines they create
activities.observe: How they hold the crayon and explore making marks.
activities.safety: Use age-appropriate non-toxic supplies and supervise to prevent mouthing.

activities.name: Caring for a Doll
activities.prepare: A large doll or plush animal and simple, safe props like a cloth or spoon.
steps: Show tucking the doll in or offering a pretend bite
Let your child lead where the story goes
Gently put words to their pretend play
activities.observe: Imaginative actions and spontaneous narration.
activities.pause: Losing interest or pushing it aside.
activities.safety: Skip tiny play utensils, long cords, or hard beads.

activities.name: Naming Everyday Feelings
activities.prepare: Real moments as they unfold during the day.
steps: Put a short, gentle phrase to their joy or frustration
Welcome the feeling without rushing it away
Hold a clear, calm boundary and offer a safe alternative
activities.observe: Gradually using gestures or words to express how they feel.
activities.pause: When big feelings peak, pause talking and offer quiet presence first.
activities.safety: Never shame, threaten, or demand they stop crying on the spot.

activities.name: Sorting Big Everyday Things
activities.prepare: Large, safe items that differ by shape, color, or use.
steps: Show sorting into two simple groups
Invite your child to sort if they are interested
Welcome their own creative ways of grouping
activities.observe: Comparing, experimenting, and explaining.
activities.safety: Skip tiny beads and magnets.

activities.name: Pretend Kitchen Play
activities.prepare: Large play pots, bowls, and soft cloth food.
steps: Make up a simple pretend menu together
Play the guest ordering a meal
Let your child play the cook preparing the dish
Weave in warm back-and-forth turns and polite words
activities.observe: Growing storylines and playful conversation.
activities.safety: Keep well clear of real knives, stoves, and hot water.

activities.name: Low Cushion Path
activities.prepare: Flat floor space and low, non-slip cushions.
steps: Lay out a simple, low path on the floor
Show stepping around or over a cushion
Let your child choose their own route
Offer a steady hand whenever they ask
activities.observe: Confident trying and growing spatial awareness.
activities.safety: Keep clear of high ledges, sharp corners, and slippery floors; stay right beside them.

activities.name: Music & Movement Together
activities.prepare: Your singing voice or music at a gentle volume.
steps: Sing a familiar, upbeat rhythm
Model simple clapping or marching
Let your child join in, improvise, and pause freely
activities.observe: Imitation and finding their own beat.
activities.pause: Tiredness or getting overly wound up.
activities.safety: Keep volume comfortable and movements gentle.

activities.name: Telling a Small Story of the Day
activities.prepare: One real moment you shared today.
steps: Recall one small thing that happened earlier
Name who was there, when it happened, and what you did
Leave unhurried space for your child to chime in
activities.observe: Remembering details and putting moments in order.
activities.pause: Not in the mood to talk.
activities.safety: Never treat retelling as a memory quiz.

activities.name: Side-by-Side Play & Turns
activities.prepare: A safe park or play space with peers nearby.
steps: Let your child watch first or play comfortably side-by-side
Model taking turns and clear, kind boundaries
Step in gently during tussles to help both children put words to their needs
activities.observe: Curiosity about peers and brief back-and-forth moments.
activities.safety: Supervise closely and check water and roadway boundaries first.

activities.name: Building Big Blocks Together
activities.prepare: Large, sturdy building blocks.
steps: Each pick a handful of blocks
Decide together what to build
Step in only when your child asks for a hand
activities.observe: Sharing ideas and figuring out how to collaborate.
activities.safety: Keep block sizes and tower heights safe for their age.

activities.name: Noticing Nature Together
activities.prepare: A safe park or neighborhood walk with trees, sky, or flowers.
steps: Walk a familiar, safe path noticing clouds, leaves, or birds
Describe small changes you spot
Let your child pick where to linger
activities.observe: Wonder, pointing, and naming.
activities.safety: Avoid touching unknown plants, berries, or insects; stay alert near traffic.

activities.name: Socks & Putting Things Away
activities.prepare: Easy-fit clothes and a low storage basket.
steps: Show just the first small step
Invite your child to try if they want
Lend a hand smoothly when needed
Notice their effort out loud
activities.observe: Pride in trying and joining daily routines.
activities.safety: Practice never replaces essential adult care and dressing.

activities.name: Picture Story Sequence
activities.prepare: 2–3 large picture cards showing a simple story.
steps: Tell the short story in order once
Invite your child to arrange or explain the cards
Welcome playful or unexpected versions
activities.observe: Sense of "first, then, next" and storytelling.
activities.safety: Use large, sturdy cards and keep it playful—never a test.

activities.name: Sharing Two Languages Naturally
activities.prepare: Everyday objects and a caregiver who speaks both languages comfortably.
steps: Connect first in the language that feels most natural at home
If you speak a second language comfortably, weave it naturally into songs or books
Respond warmly in whichever language your child uses
activities.observe: Eagerness to communicate and understanding in context.
activities.pause: If it ever feels forced or tiring for you or your child.
activities.safety: Skip vocabulary drills; never delay a speech check if you have communication concerns.

activities.name: Family Photos & Names
activities.prepare: Sturdy family photos or a small photo album.
steps: Point to familiar relatives and friends
Connect photos to real visits and video calls
Let your child turn pages and point
activities.observe: Looking closely, pointing, and asking questions.
activities.safety: Protect your child's privacy—avoid sharing private details publicly online.

activities.name: Stop, Look & Hold Hands
activities.prepare: A safe sidewalk observation spot or toy cars at home.
steps: Model "stop, look, hold hands" in a safe setting
Act it out playfully with toy cars
Always keep an adult fully in charge near real roads
activities.observe: Recognizing and echoing simple safety words.
activities.safety: Never let a toddler practice road safety alone.

activities.name: Family Stories & Traditions
activities.prepare: Holiday photos, family stories, or safe seasonal keepsakes.
steps: Share a true family story or holiday memory
Weave in familiar songs, favorite foods, and everyday scenes
Follow your child's curiosity
activities.observe: Joining in and asking about family traditions.
activities.safety: Keep seasonal foods, decorations, batteries, and ribbons age-safe.

blocks.text: **A gentle note:** WHO sleep ranges are population-level guides, not a diagnosis for an individual child's sleep challenges. Build awake tummy time gradually in short stretches as your baby tolerates it—tummy time is for awake play, while sleep always starts on the back. At 36 months, children move into the WHO 3–4 year group. Source: WHO *Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age*.

items: **Back to sleep:** Under 12 months, place your baby on their back for every sleep on a firm, flat, level surface—clear of pillows, loose blankets, crib bumpers, and toys.

**Supervised tummy time:** Offer awake tummy time on a safe floor surface with an adult right beside them. If your baby grows tired, falls asleep, or seems uncomfortable, move them to their safe sleep space.

**Stay ahead of new movement:** Each time rolling, sitting, pulling to stand, climbing, or running emerges, recheck heights, stair gates, anchored furniture, windows, medicines, hot surfaces, and water—never rely on "they can't reach that yet."
**Note & check in:** If you notice a fall, persistent one-sided posture, or a clear loss of motor skills, jot it down and check in with your pediatrician.

blocks.text: Sources: AAP *Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations*; WHO *Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age*; China NHC *Early Childhood Development Service Guidelines (Trial)*.

items: **When to begin:** Most babies start solids around 6 months when they show readiness—steady head and neck control, sitting with support, and interest in food. For preterm babies or those with medical or allergy considerations, follow your pediatrician's timing.
**How to offer:** Match textures and piece sizes to your child's current skills. Keep them seated upright with an adult watching closely, and let them stop when they signal they are full.
**Variety alongside milk:** Solids complement breast milk or formula rather than replacing it right away. Follow local pediatric guidance for iron-rich foods and introducing common allergens.

**Preventing choking:** Avoid whole grapes, cherry tomatoes, whole nuts, raw hard carrots, popcorn, and thick globs of nut butter. Follow CDC choking-prevention guidance for cutting and softening foods.
**If an emergency happens:** Signs of choking, trouble breathing, or a severe allergic reaction call for immediate local emergency care—never delay treatment.

blocks.text: Sources: WHO *Guideline for complementary feeding of infants and young children 6–23 months of age*; CDC *When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods*; CDC *Choking Hazards, Infant and Toddler Nutrition*.

items: **Oral care:** As soon as the first tooth appears, brush gently using an age-appropriate amount of fluoride toothpaste as recommended by local pediatric dental guidance, and schedule regular checkups.
**Screens:** WHO advises against sedentary screen time for infants and 1-year-olds, and caps it at 1 hour a day (less is better) for 2- and 3-year-olds. A cap is a ceiling, not a daily target.

**Home languages:** Speak and read in whichever languages you know best—whether one language, a local dialect, or several. Growing up with more than one language does not cause speech delays; if communication concerns ever arise, seek an evaluation that considers all the languages your child hears.

**Seek emergency care right away:** Trouble breathing, unresponsiveness, signs of severe choking, an acute allergic reaction, or any life-threatening symptom calls for immediate local emergency services—do not wait to observe or log.

**Check in promptly:** Reach out to your pediatrician or child health clinic if your child loses a skill they once had, rarely responds to sound, consistently favors one side, struggles significantly with feeding, raises ongoing communication concerns, or if something simply feels off to you. Evaluations may include hearing, vision, and developmental checks.
**Follow your care plan:** If a specialist shares findings or recommendations, keep their notes and follow-up dates handy—medical guidance always takes priority over home play plans.

health.text: China's National Immunization Program schedules routine vaccines by completed month: Hepatitis B dose 1 and BCG at birth; Hepatitis B dose 2 at 1 month; IPV at 2 and 3 months; DTaP at 2, 4, 6, and 18 months; MMR at 8 and 18 months; Meningococcal A at 6 and 9 months; Japanese Encephalitis at 8 months and 2 years; Hepatitis A at 18 months; and Meningococcal AC at 3 years. Check your local pediatric schedule if you live elsewhere.

Well-child visits track weight, length (or height), and head circumference. China's Growth Standards for Children Under 7 use these three core measures to follow your child's own curve over time—a single reading on its own is never the whole story.

Begin daily vitamin D supplementation (400 IU) soon after birth. For preterm, low-birth-weight, or multiple-birth infants, Chinese clinical consensus recommends 800 IU daily starting at 1 week, then 400 IU after 3 months. Always confirm the dose with your pediatrician.

health.topic: When to Call About a Fever
health.text: Under 3 months, a temperature of 38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher calls for immediate medical advice. At any age, seek urgent care for temperatures repeatedly above 40°C (104°F), marked lethargy or inconsolable fussiness, a stiff neck, trouble breathing, an unexplained rash, repeated vomiting or diarrhea, or a seizure. Contact your doctor if a fever lasts more than 24 hours under age 2, or more than 3 days at age 2 and up.

Use a properly installed child car seat from the very first ride. Keep your child rear-facing as long as possible, up to the seat's highest weight or height limit. Never place a rear-facing seat in front of an active passenger airbag. Harness straps should sit at or below the shoulders with no slack to pinch, and the chest clip should rest at armpit level.

Perinatal depression screening is part of routine prenatal and postpartum care in China, and the AAP recommends screening mothers at the 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month well-child visits (such as with the EPDS). If a caregiver feels persistently low, overwhelmed, unable to care for themselves or the baby, or has thoughts of harming themselves or the child, reach out for medical support right away.

rows.do: Speak naturally about one thing you are doing as you hold, change, or feed your baby. Pause after they coo to leave room for a turn. Reading a book can be as simple as pausing on one picture and naming it.
rows.notice: Turning toward voices, steady gaze, and early sounds beyond crying—always honoring sleep and comfort first.

rows.do: Echo your baby's vowels and coos in gentle back-and-forth turns. Name real objects in context ("This is your cup") and follow their gaze to match your voice to their interest.
rows.notice: Natural vocal turns, sustained attention, and locating sounds—no quizzing on specific words.

rows.do: Play short "I speak, you answer" sound games. Follow what your baby looks at, point and name it, and pair everyday gestures like waving.
rows.notice: Varied babbling syllables, clear intent to connect, and responding to their name. Check in with a professional if anything worries you.

rows.do: Put words to your baby's points and reaches. Use consistent names and goodbye rituals in real moments, and let them turn the sturdy pages of board books.
rows.notice: Gestures, understanding simple everyday words, and active requests—never pressuring them to repeat words on cue.

rows.do: Echo your child's words and gently expand them into clear, simple phrases. Name objects and let them respond in their own way, weaving language into real daily tasks.
rows.notice: Word attempts, following a word paired with a gesture, and pointing to ask for help.

rows.do: Talk about actions in familiar picture books. When they say "ball," reply "You want the red ball." Model simple, respectful phrases like "please," "no thanks," and "your turn."
rows.notice: Two-word combinations, following simple one-step directions, and enjoyment of books and back-and-forth talk.

rows.do: Talk about people and actions in storybooks and invite your child to describe what they see in their own words. Listen closely to their everyday choices.
rows.notice: Growing vocabulary, pronouns, action words, and two-step directions—using the 30-month CDC checklist as a gentle reference rather than a word-count race.

rows.do: Line up family photos in order and take turns telling the story. Stay with a conversation for two or more turns, using open-ended questions about pictures and daily life.
rows.notice: How clearly familiar and unfamiliar adults understand them, back-and-forth conversation, and asking for help. Seek an evaluation if you have ongoing concerns.

rows.do: Offer safe, supervised floor time while awake. Build brief tummy time gradually without forcing, and vary your baby's view while holding them securely.
rows.notice: Comfort during play, head-lifting attempts, and balanced movement on both sides. Always place on their back to sleep.

rows.do: Place a large, safe toy to the left or right on a floor mat and wait for your baby to turn, reach, or try rolling on their own, with plenty of room to rest.
rows.notice: Head control, propping on forearms, and smooth limb coordination—avoid pulling them into a sit or forcing rolls.

rows.do: Give generous floor space so your baby can roll, pivot, sit, or scoot in their own way. Clear hazards and stay close for quiet safety.
rows.notice: How they shift positions and stay curious—every crawling or scooting style is valid.

rows.do: Offer sturdy furniture to pull up on and low-risk floor spaces to explore. Let them shift postures and fetch toys independently, skipping baby walkers.
rows.notice: Pulling to stand, safe cruising, and rechecking furniture stability as their reach grows.

rows.do: Roll a ball on flat ground, push a sturdy walker-wagon, and take short unhurried walks outside. Keep floor play welcoming for children still building walking confidence.
rows.notice: Eagerness to move, fall safety, and comfort—without setting a deadline for first steps.

rows.do: Kick and roll soft balls, run on open flat ground, and weave around low cushions. Stay within easy reach and let them change direction freely.
rows.notice: How they pace themselves and pause to rest—always staying well clear of water and roadways.

rows.do: Weave kicking, running, and open outdoor play throughout the day to break up sitting, following WHO's 1–2 year movement rhythm.
rows.notice: Total daily movement, outdoor safety, and signs of tiredness—play time is not a structured workout.

rows.do: Add direction changes, gentle two-foot jumps, chasing balls, and safe playground exploration. At 36 months, transition to the WHO 3–4 year movement group.
rows.notice: Joy in joining play, growing safety awareness, and fatigue cues—never ranking athletic skill.

rows.do: Let your awake baby study your face, their hands, and simple high-contrast images. Keep toys washable and too large to swallow, waiting for natural gaze and open hands.
rows.notice: Brief focus and visual curiosity; check with a doctor if visual tracking seems persistently difficult.

rows.do: Place lightweight toys within easy reach so your baby can bat, grasp, and release. Offer visual interest on both sides without forcing objects into their fist.
rows.notice: Watching their hands, touching, and moving from looking to intentional reaching—with material safety first.

rows.do: Offer two large objects to bang and pass hand-to-hand, and model putting things into and out of a bowl. Supervise closely as they explore safely with their mouth.
rows.notice: Transferring objects, banging, reaching, and looking for dropped toys—skip sensory bottles with tiny loose parts.

rows.do: Hide a large toy under a cloth while they watch and wait for them to uncover it. Drop blocks into a container and invite them to try.
rows.notice: Searching, placing in, pincer grasp, and object exploration—keeping any finger foods strictly choking-safe.

rows.do: Stack large, safe blocks and model real uses for a cup, phone, or book. When a tower tumbles, give them space to try again on their own.
rows.notice: Imitating everyday object uses, stacking, and early scribbling—leaving play open-ended if interest shifts.

rows.do: Pair two toys together (like a doll and a spoon) and offer simple cause-and-effect toys. Encourage them to figure out how things work at their own pace.
rows.notice: Early pretend play, using two hands together, and problem-solving—keeping small parts out of reach.

rows.do: Sort large everyday items, twist safe lids, and tidy up in a simple order—letting your child invent their own sorting rules.
rows.notice: Two-step actions, problem-solving, and noticing colors—without turning play into repetitive quizzing.

rows.do: Build simple bridges with large blocks and rebuild after they fall. Model drawing a circle, threading chunky beads, or putting simple picture cards in order.
rows.notice: Sharing their ideas and sticking with a challenge—keep any threading pieces large and closely supervised.

rows.do: Respond steadily to cries and tired cues with predictable holding and soothing. Match touch and facial expressions to your baby's comfort.
rows.notice: What helps them settle, early social smiles, and making sure caregivers get rest and support too.

rows.do: Answer spontaneous smiles, coos, and gazes. Play brief face-to-face expression games with familiar family members, keeping stimulation gentle.
rows.notice: How they invite interaction, signal they need a break, and respond to familiar faces.

rows.do: Play gentle peekaboo and let your baby set the pace for more or all done. Stay close as a steady anchor when unfamiliar people are nearby.
rows.notice: Joy, wariness, and how they seek you out—honoring separation feelings as a healthy sign of bond.

rows.do: Weave waving, clapping, and handing objects into real moments. Say a simple, warm goodbye before brief separations so your return feels predictable.
rows.notice: Initiating gestures or shared games—never testing attachment by slipping away unexpectedly.

rows.do: Model respecting "no," asking for help, and offering a toy. With other toddlers, set out matching materials for comfortable side-by-side play.
rows.notice: Showing you favorite things, simple imitation, and turning to you when frustrated.

rows.do: Name everyday feelings—angry, sad, glad—in plain words. When conflicts arise, keep bodies safe first, then model asking, taking turns, and gentle alternatives.
rows.notice: Interest in peers, how they respond to feeling words, and what helps them recover.

rows.do: Invite side-by-side play and brief shared building with peers. Teach both how to ask for a turn and how to step away when they need space.
rows.notice: Parallel play, moments of cooperation, and willingness to join—never judging character by how quickly a toddler shares.

rows.do: Play pretend store or doctor together. Agree on 2–3 clear, visible safety rules together, and offer calm words when frustration hits.
rows.notice: Joining peer play, calming with support, and asking for help. Reach out to a professional for persistent concerns.

rows.do: Pair feeding, diapering, and bedtime settling with calm, simple words. Prioritize parent recovery and baby's health, honoring all languages spoken at home.
rows.notice: Steady feeding and rest rhythms, and whether caregivers have the support they need.

rows.do: Build familiar everyday words during baths, dressing, and lifting. Sing rhymes or lullabies naturally in whichever language(s) feel like home.
rows.notice: Your baby's delight in familiar voices, rhythms, and songs.

rows.do: Use a safe, upright high chair and respond to hunger and fullness cues—opening wide, closing lips, turning away. Share family rhymes and songs.
rows.notice: Comfortable swallowing, readiness for textures, and checking with your pediatrician when unsure.

rows.do: Practice sips from an open cup with your hands steadying it, turn board-book pages, and wave goodbye. Everyday household words matter far more than flashcards.
rows.notice: Curious attempts to do things themselves.

rows.do: Invite them to hold a sock, drop a toy in a basket, or carry a napkin. Demonstrate slowly and wait for them to join—completion is never the goal.
rows.notice: Small choices and willingness to cooperate, knowing they still rely on your steady help.

rows.do: Pause during dressing so they can push an arm or foot through, hold a spoon, or put a toy back. Share family holidays and stories through everyday moments.
rows.notice: Asking for help, eagerness to pitch in, and pride in doing part of a routine.

rows.do: Invite them to set napkins, tidy toys, or pull off loose clothes. Talk about familiar routines naturally in your home language(s) without forcing vocabulary quotas.
rows.notice: Following short routine sequences, using everyday words, and trying independently.

rows.do: Use family photos to tell stories in order, and encourage multi-step dressing and tidying. Approach toilet learning gently based on physical and emotional readiness.
rows.notice: Where a gentle reminder helps, and their willingness to participate and accept support.

rows.do: Place baby on their back on a firm, flat, clear surface for every sleep. Keep floor play awake and supervised, and follow local newborn and 1-month checkups.
rows.notice: WHO sleep 14–17 hours; local pediatric care comes first; follow regional newborn follow-up schedules.

rows.do: Maintain safe sleep habits and fall-proof active floor play. Watch for sitting and head-control readiness around 6 months before starting solids with pediatric guidance.
rows.notice: WHO 4–11 month sleep 12–16 hours; CDC 4- & 6-month checklists; China 3- & 6-month check-ins.

rows.do: Start solids when developmentally ready, keeping textures safe, seating upright, and supervision constant alongside milk feeds. Watch for allergies and choking risks.
rows.notice: China 8-month check-in; AAP/CDC 9-month developmental milestone & screening visit; raise health questions early.

rows.do: Cruising and pulling up raise fall and burn risks—update food cutting, anchor furniture, and lock away medicines as new skills arrive.
rows.notice: CDC & China 12-month check-ins; always supervise early open-cup practice.

rows.do: Follow WHO 1–2 year guidance: at least 180 minutes of varied daily movement, 11–14 hours of sleep, and no sedentary screen time at age 1.
rows.notice: CDC 15-month checklist; China & AAP 18-month developmental and autism screening.

rows.do: Walking and running expand your toddler's world—stay vigilant around water, streets, small objects, and heights, and always eat seated.
rows.notice: China 24-month check-in; AAP 24-month autism and behavioral-emotional screening.

rows.do: WHO caps age-2 screen time at 1 hour (less is better), alongside 180 minutes of daily movement and 11–14 hours of sleep. Keep up toothbrushing and outdoor safety.
rows.notice: China 30-month check-in, CDC 30-month checklist, and AAP developmental screening; follow local clinical schedules.

rows.do: Continue the WHO 12–35 month rhythm through 35 months; at 36 months, shift to the 3–4 year group (10–13 hours sleep, 180 minutes movement with 60 minutes moderate-to-vigorous).
rows.notice: China 36-month check-in, CDC 36-month checklist, and AAP behavioral-emotional screening; plan upcoming preschool and care visits.

confidence.text: **Source alignment levels (not statistical confidence intervals or GRADE):** H means directly supported by an official guideline at the matching age; M means the general direction is supported while specific activities remain flexible; L means Montessori-inspired or practical home-play design without single-activity trial proof; U means unverified, conflicting, or unsupported.

**Review status:** Verified against official pages or summaries / carried from cited references / home-play arrangement / confirm with local pediatrician / no direct trial evidence. A guidance point can carry both a strong institutional recommendation and lower certainty for a specific play variation.

**Honoring uncertainty:** No evidence says every child should hit the exact same movement, word count, or play length in the same month. Outside WHO's age-group daily rhythms, we never set strict minute quotas for individual home activities.
